cwes.name: Improper Control of Generation of Code
Improper Encoding or Escaping of Output

1.description:
### Impact

A Gradle [version catalog](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/version_catalogs.html) declares the versions, dependency coordinates and plugin ids a build uses. A build defines its own catalogs in `gradle/libs.versions.toml`, in other TOML files or in the settings script, and can import catalogs published to a repository. Gradle generates type-safe accessors for each catalog, such as `libs.guava`, by generating Java source, compiling it, and loading it while the settings are evaluated. This advisory is about a vulnerability in the generation of version catalog accessors.

Gradle writes catalog values into the generated source without escaping them. A version, dependency coordinate or plugin id crafted for this adds code to the accessor classes, and that code runs when Gradle loads the catalog, with the privileges of the user running the build. It runs in every build that imports or defines the catalog, before any build script, including when an IDE synchronizes the project, even when the build uses none of the catalog's entries. This can expose the secrets available to the build, including repository and publishing credentials. This has been demonstrated with a proof-of-concept. This advisory does not publish the proof-of-concept.

Builds that import a published version catalog are the most at risk. Its publisher, or anyone able to publish a version of it that the build resolves, can run code in the build, while importing a catalog is expected to run no code. Dependency verification does not prevent this when it accepts the catalog version that carries the payload. Users who review an untrusted project before building it or opening it in an IDE are also at risk, since the code is in a catalog file and not in a build script. Commands that evaluate no settings, such as `gradle --version`, are not affected.

The attacker does not need access to the machine running the build: publishing a catalog the build imports is enough.

### Patches

Gradle now rejects version catalog entries that contain `*/` or `\u`. This covers versions (including strict, preferred and rejected versions, and branches), groups, names and plugin ids. The build fails while the catalog is loaded, before any accessor is generated, with a problem such as `In version catalog libs, on alias 'example' version '…' contains '*/', which is not allowed`. Gradle also escapes these sequences in other text it copies into the generated accessors, such as a catalog's description. No valid version, coordinate or plugin id contains them, so valid catalogs are not affected.

| Fix version | Availability |
| ---------- | ----------- |
| 9.9.1 | OSS |
| 9.8.3 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |
| 9.7.3 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |
| 9.6.3 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |
| 9.5.3 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |
| 9.4.3 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |
| 9.3.3 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |
| 9.2.3 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |
| 8.14.7 | OSS |
| 7.6.8 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |

### Workarounds

Upgrading Gradle is our recommended fix.

If you cannot upgrade immediately:

* **Check the values of every version catalog a build imports or defines.** This covers `gradle/libs.versions.toml`, other catalog files, catalogs defined in the settings script, and the TOML file of each published catalog the settings script imports. No valid version, group, name or plugin id contains `*/` or `\u`; do not build, or open in an IDE, a project whose catalogs contain them. For local files:

  ```
  grep -rn -e '\*/' -e '\\u' --include='*.toml' .
  ```

* **Import published catalogs at a fixed, checked version.** Do not import a catalog with a dynamic version (`1.+`, `latest.release`) or a changing one (`-SNAPSHOT`), which picks up new content with no change to the build. With [dependency verification](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/securing_dependencies.html), a different file published under the checked version then fails the build.

### Forensics

Gradle keeps the source it generates for catalog accessors in the Gradle user home, under `caches/<Gradle version>/dependencies-accessors/`. A value that adds code shows as text after the end of a comment, `*/`, on a line of that source:

    grep -rnE '\*/.*[^[:space:]]' ~/.gradle/caches/*/dependencies-accessors/

The catalog files themselves, and their history in version control, show the same values.

After upgrading, a build that fails with `… contains '*/', which is not allowed` or `… contains '\u', which is not allowed` declares a catalog carrying a payload.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> The lack of such traces cannot be used to conclude no such attack was performed. Their presence is not a confirmation that an attack happened, but an indication that more investigations are needed.

### References

* [Version catalogs](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/version_catalogs.html)
* [Verifying dependencies](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/securing_dependencies.html)

More about this type of vulnerabilities:

* https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/94.html
* https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/116.html

1.description:
### Impact

[TestKit](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/test_kit.html) runs Gradle builds from tests and from build logic, mostly to test Gradle plugins. Its `GradleRunner` uses a dedicated directory, the TestKit directory, as the Gradle user home of the builds it runs. It holds their `gradle.properties`, init scripts, dependency caches and daemon registry. This advisory is about a vulnerability in TestKit.

When the TestKit directory is not configured, and `GradleRunner` does not run in Gradle's `Test` task, TestKit uses `.gradle-test-kit` in the temporary directory of the JVM, given by the `java.io.tmpdir` system property. On Linux this is `/tmp` by default, so the directory is `/tmp/.gradle-test-kit`. The path is the same for every user, and TestKit uses an existing directory at that path as long as it can write to it, whoever owns it. A local attacker who creates that directory before the victim does controls the Gradle user home of the victim's TestKit builds. Gradle loads the `gradle.properties` and init scripts it finds in that directory. Files the attacker places there therefore run code with the privileges of the user running the build, and expose the secrets available to it.

[GHSA-89qm-pxvm-p336](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/security/advisories/GHSA-89qm-pxvm-p336) (CVE-2021-29428) reported this vulnerability for Gradle versions before 7.0, where TestKit always used `.gradle-test-kit-<user name>` in the system temporary directory. Its fix was incomplete. Since Gradle 7.0, tests run by Gradle's `Test` task use a TestKit directory in the build directory, and are not affected. The system temporary directory remains in use when:

* build logic or a plugin calls `GradleRunner` from a task or a worker action, so in the Gradle daemon or a worker process;
* tests run in an IDE's own test runner rather than through Gradle.

Builds running on **shared, multi-user Linux hosts** are the most at risk, such as CI agents running jobs as different users. The attacker can create the directory before the victim's first TestKit build on the host, or whenever it is removed afterwards, for instance by `systemd-tmpfiles` or at reboot when `/tmp` is a `tmpfs`. Windows and macOS use a temporary directory per user and are not affected. Neither are Linux setups giving each user or job a private `/tmp`.

This vulnerability is not exploitable from a remote network connection.

### Patches

When the TestKit directory is not configured and `GradleRunner` does not run in Gradle's `Test` task, TestKit now uses `.gradle-test-kit-<user name>` in the system temporary directory, and creates it accessible to its owner only.

If that path already exists, TestKit uses it only when it is a real directory, rather than a symbolic link, that belongs to the current user and that no other user can write to. Otherwise, TestKit leaves it untouched, does not run the build, and fails with `Unable to use <path> as the TestKit directory: <reason>.`

A TestKit directory set with `GradleRunner.withTestKitDir()` or the `org.gradle.testkit.dir` system property, and the one used under Gradle's `Test` task, are unchanged. The previous `.gradle-test-kit` directory in the system temporary directory is no longer used and can be deleted.

| Fix version | Availability |
| ---------- | ----------- |
| 9.9.2 | OSS |
| 9.8.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |
| 9.7.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |
| 9.6.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |
| 9.5.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |
| 9.4.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |
| 9.3.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |
| 9.2.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |
| 8.14.8 | OSS |
| 7.6.9 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |

### Workarounds

Upgrading Gradle is our recommended fix.

If you cannot upgrade immediately:

* **Set the TestKit directory explicitly.** Call [`GradleRunner.withTestKitDir()`](https://docs.gradle.org/current/javadoc/org/gradle/testkit/runner/GradleRunner.html#withTestKitDir(java.io.File)) with a directory only you can write to, for example in the build directory, or set the `org.gradle.testkit.dir` system property in the JVM that runs `GradleRunner`. For an IDE test runner, add `-Dorg.gradle.testkit.dir=PATH` to the JVM options of the run configuration.
* **Run tests through Gradle's `Test` task**, which places the TestKit directory in the build directory since Gradle 7.0.
* **Do not run builds on shared, multi-user machines**, or give each user or job a private temporary directory.

### Forensics

TestKit never creates `gradle.properties` or an `init.d` directory in the TestKit directory. On Linux, check the owner and permissions of the directory and look for these files. Before Gradle 7.0, the directory is `/tmp/.gradle-test-kit-<user name>`. Adjust the path if `java.io.tmpdir` is set to another directory.

    ls -la /tmp/.gradle-test-kit /tmp/.gradle-test-kit/init.d
    cat /tmp/.gradle-test-kit/gradle.properties

A directory owned by another user, writable by other users, or containing files you did not create indicates an attempt.

A TestKit build failing with `Unable to write to test kit directory: /tmp/.gradle-test-kit` means that another user created the directory first, maliciously or not.

A fixed version reports a directory it refuses instead of using it: `Unable to use /tmp/.gradle-test-kit-<user name> as the TestKit directory: it is owned by another user.` The other reasons are `it is a symbolic link`, `it is not a directory` and `it is writable by other users`.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> The lack of such traces cannot be used to conclude no such attack was performed. Their presence is not a confirmation that an attack happened, but an indication that more investigations are needed.

### References

* [Testing Build Logic with TestKit](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/test_kit.html)
* Prior Gradle vulnerabilities: [GHSA-89qm-pxvm-p336](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/security/advisories/GHSA-89qm-pxvm-p336), [GHSA-465q-w4mf-4f4r](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/security/advisories/GHSA-465q-w4mf-4f4r)

More about this type of vulnerabilities:

* https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/379.html
* https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/283.html

Inclusion of Functionality from Untrusted Control Sphere

1.description:
### Impact

Gradle's [dependency verification](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/securing_dependencies.html) checks every dependency and plugin a build downloads against checksums and trusted signing keys recorded in `gradle/verification-metadata.xml`. Once that file is written and reviewed, a build fails if a dependency is replaced by different content, for instance after a repository compromise. Changing modules, such as `-SNAPSHOT` versions, are [excluded](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/securing_dependencies.html#sec:verification-scope) because their content changes by design. This advisory is about a vulnerability in dependency verification.

The exclusion also applies to changing modules that a build does not declare itself, but reaches through the metadata of another dependency. When a release the build depends on declares a dependency on a `-SNAPSHOT` version, Gradle verifies the release but neither verifies the snapshot nor records anything for it when generating `verification-metadata.xml`. Reviewing the changes to that file does not reveal the snapshot.

An attacker who publishes such a release, or who controls the coordinates of the snapshot it depends on, can serve harmless content while the release is reviewed and adopted, then replace the snapshot at any later time. Every later build resolves the new content without a verification failure. When the snapshot is on the classpath of a plugin or of build logic, or its code is run by a task such as tests, the attacker's code runs with the privileges of the user running the build. This exposes the secrets available to the build, including repository and publishing credentials.

Only builds that use dependency verification are affected: a build without it does not verify any dependency, snapshot or not. Among those, builds that declare a repository serving snapshots, such as a snapshot repository, JitPack or an internal repository manager proxying one, are at risk. Maven Central does not serve snapshots, and Gradle does not use repositories declared in POM files, so a build resolving only from Maven Central is not exposed. The Gradle Plugin Portal does not support snapshots either: the content of a version published there cannot change, even when the version is named `-SNAPSHOT`, so plugins and dependencies resolved from it cannot be replaced this way.

### Patches

With dependency verification enabled, Gradle now verifies changing modules like any other module, whether the build declares them itself or reaches them through another dependency. Their metadata and artifacts are checked against `verification-metadata.xml`, and `--write-verification-metadata` records them.

This changes the behavior of builds that use dependency verification and resolve changing modules, including snapshots they declare themselves. Such a build fails with `Dependency verification failed` until its changing modules are covered by `verification-metadata.xml`. The checksum of a snapshot changes each time it is published, so prefer [verifying signatures](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/securing_dependencies.html#sec:signature-verification) and trusting the keys that sign them. Snapshots you accept without verification must be [trusted explicitly](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/securing_dependencies.html#sec:trusting-artifacts), which makes the exemption visible to reviewers of that file:

```xml
<trusted-artifacts>
   <trust group="com.example" version=".*-SNAPSHOT" regex="true"/>
</trusted-artifacts>
```

| Fix version | Availability |
| ---------- | ----------- |
| 9.9.2 | OSS |
| 9.8.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |
| 9.7.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |
| 9.6.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |
| 9.5.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |
| 9.4.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |
| 9.3.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |
| 9.2.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |
| 8.14.8 | OSS |
| 7.6.9 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |

### Workarounds

Upgrading Gradle is our recommended fix.

If you cannot upgrade immediately:

* **Fail the build on changing versions.** [`failOnChangingVersions()`](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/resolution_rules.html#sec:conflict-resolution-strategy) rejects changing modules anywhere in the dependency graph, including those brought in by other dependencies. Apply it to the build script classpath as well, for example in an init script:

  ```kotlin
  allprojects {
      configurations.configureEach {
          resolutionStrategy.failOnChangingVersions()
      }
      buildscript.configurations.configureEach {
          resolutionStrategy.failOnChangingVersions()
      }
  }
  ```

  It cannot be combined with dependency locking on the same configuration.

* **Restrict what snapshot repositories can serve.** Use [repository content filtering](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/filtering_repository_content.html) to limit each repository that serves snapshots to the groups you expect from it, and declare the other repositories with `mavenContent { releasesOnly() }`.

### Forensics

Snapshots in the dependency graph are listed with a `-SNAPSHOT` version in the output of `gradle dependencies` and in build scans. `gradle dependencyInsight --dependency MODULE` shows which dependency brought a given snapshot in.

The Gradle dependency cache keeps each downloaded file under `<Gradle user home>/caches/modules-2/files-2.1/<group>/<module>/<version>/<sha1>/`. Several `<sha1>` directories under a snapshot version show that its content changed over time.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> The lack of such traces cannot be used to conclude no such attack was performed. Their presence is not a confirmation that an attack happened, but an indication that more investigations are needed.

### References

* [Verifying dependencies](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/securing_dependencies.html)
* [Filtering repository content](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/filtering_repository_content.html)

More about this type of vulnerabilities:

* https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/494.html
* https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/829.html
1.summary: Transitive snapshot dependencies skip dependency verification

cwes.name: Key Exchange without Entity Authentication
Download of Code Without Integrity Check

1.description:
### Impact

Gradle can resolve dependencies from, and publish to, Maven and Ivy repositories accessed over **SFTP** (`sftp://` URLs), authenticating with a username and password. SSH authenticates the server to the client with the server's host key, which the client checks against the keys it already knows, usually in `~/.ssh/known_hosts`. This advisory is about a vulnerability in how Gradle connects to SFTP repositories.

Gradle accepts any host key presented by the server. It does not read `known_hosts`, and no setting enables verification. An attacker who can make the build connect to them instead of the real server, through an on-path network position, DNS or ARP spoofing, or by taking over the address of a decommissioned server, can impersonate the repository without any warning to the user. The attacker can then:

* obtain the repository password, which Gradle sends as its only authentication method. Credentials of a publishing repository give write access to that repository, and to everything that consumes it;
* serve arbitrary module metadata, plugins and jars, which run in the build with the privileges of the user running it;
* alter or swallow artifacts being published.

Checksum files fetched from the repository offer no protection, since the attacker serves them too. Builds using [dependency verification](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/securing_dependencies.html) detect substituted artifacts that are already listed in their verification metadata, but not the theft of the repository password, nor tampering with publications.

Only builds that declare an `sftp://` repository are affected. A demonstration against Gradle's test SFTP server shows a build succeeding, and sending the password, after the server's host key was replaced.

### Patches

Gradle now verifies the host key of SFTP repository servers against the OpenSSH known hosts files: `~/.ssh/known_hosts` and `/etc/ssh/ssh_known_hosts`, or `%ProgramData%\ssh\ssh_known_hosts` on Windows. A connection to a server whose host is not listed, or whose key does not match the one listed, fails before the repository credentials are sent. The error names the server, the type and SHA-256 fingerprint of the key it presented, and how to add it.

This changes the behavior of builds that use SFTP repositories. Gradle does not record the key of a server it connects to for the first time, so the host key of every SFTP repository server must be listed before the build runs. Check the fingerprint with the server's administrator, then add the key, for example with `ssh-keyscan -p <port> <host> >> ~/.ssh/known_hosts`. Host certificates (`@cert-authority` entries) and wildcard host patterns are not supported.

To keep connecting to a server without verifying its host key, set [`allowInsecureProtocol = true`](https://docs.gradle.org/current/dsl/org.gradle.api.artifacts.repositories.UrlArtifactRepository.html#org.gradle.api.artifacts.repositories.UrlArtifactRepository:allowInsecureProtocol) on the repository. That repository then remains exposed to this vulnerability.

| Fix version | Availability |
| ---------- | ----------- |
| 9.9.2 | OSS |
| 9.8.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |
| 9.7.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |
| 9.6.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |
| 9.5.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |
| 9.4.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |
| 9.3.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |
| 9.2.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |
| 8.14.8 | OSS |
| 7.6.9 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |

### Workarounds

Upgrading Gradle is our recommended fix.

If you cannot upgrade immediately:

* **Move to an HTTPS repository.** Gradle validates the server certificate of HTTPS repositories against the JVM trust store.
* **Enable dependency verification, ideally with signature verification.** It detects substituted artifacts for dependencies whose checksums or signing keys were recorded before the attack. It does not protect repository credentials or publications.
* **Use separate, least-privilege credentials** for resolving and for publishing, and only provide publishing credentials to the builds that publish.

### Forensics

Gradle does not log the host key of SFTP servers above debug level. With `--debug`, the SSH library logs the host and the key type it accepted, but not the key fingerprint, and only when the first SFTP connection of the Gradle daemon was made at debug level.

To check whether resolved artifacts were substituted, compare the files in the Gradle dependency cache with the repository over a trusted channel. The cache stores each file under `<Gradle user home>/caches/modules-2/files-2.1/<group>/<module>/<version>/<sha1>/`, where `<sha1>` is the SHA-1 checksum of the file as it was downloaded.

To check publications, compare the artifacts on the repository server with the build outputs, and check the server's authentication logs for the publishing account: a publication that reported success but left no login on the server reached another host.

A fixed version reports a server it cannot authenticate instead of connecting to it. `Could not verify the identity of SFTP server at sftp://<host>:<port>: its key does not match the one listed for this host in the SSH known hosts files.` means that the key of a known server changed, through a legitimate key rotation or an impersonation attempt. The message includes the fingerprint of the presented key, to compare with the one of the real server.

If an SFTP repository was used over a network you do not fully trust, rotate its credentials.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> The lack of such traces cannot be used to conclude no such attack was performed. Their presence is not a confirmation that an attack happened, but an indication that more investigations are needed.

### References

* [Supported repository protocols](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/supported_repository_protocols.html)
* [Verifying dependencies](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/securing_dependencies.html)

More about this type of vulnerabilities:

* https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/322.html
* https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/494.html

cwes.name: Incorrect Default Permissions
Concurrent Execution using Shared Resource with Improper Synchronization

1.description:
### Impact

A **Gradle client** (the `gradle`/`gradlew` CLI or an IDE using the Tooling API) finds running **Gradle daemons** through a registry file, `daemon/<Gradle version>/registry.bin` in the Gradle user home. For each daemon, the registry records its loopback address and the secret token that authenticates clients to it. Anyone holding a token can connect to that daemon and have it run a build as the user who started it. The registry is meant to be readable by its owner only. This advisory is about a vulnerability in how the registry file is created.

When the first daemon of a given Gradle version starts, Gradle creates the version directory and the registry file with the default permissions of the process, which on most Linux and macOS systems let other users read them. Gradle restricts both to the owner right afterwards, then writes the registry content. Another local user who opens the registry file within that window keeps a handle to it that remains readable after the permissions change, and reads the daemon tokens written afterwards. Since the file is rewritten in place, the same handle also reads every later update, so the attacker obtains the token of every daemon of that Gradle version for as long as the file exists.

With a token, the attacker can submit a build to the victim's daemon, which runs code with the privileges of the user running the build and exposes in-memory and on-disk secrets available to it.

Builds running on **shared / multi-user build hosts** are the most at risk. The attacker must be able to traverse every directory down to the registry file. Gradle does not restrict the permissions of the Gradle user home when it creates it, so whether other users can reach it depends on the user's home directory and umask. A Gradle user home, or home directory, that other users cannot enter prevents the attack. The window only exists when the first daemon of a Gradle version starts in a given Gradle user home.

This vulnerability is not exploitable from a remote network connection.

### Patches

Gradle now creates the daemon registry and its directory with owner-only permissions in the call that creates them. There is no longer a window during which other users can open the registry.

Each update of the daemon registry now atomically replaces the file with a new one instead of rewriting it in place. A handle opened on an earlier registry file does not read the tokens written afterwards.

| Fix version | Availability |
| ---------- | ----------- |
| 9.9.2 | OSS |
| 9.8.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |
| 9.7.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |
| 9.6.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |
| 9.5.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |
| 9.4.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |
| 9.3.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |
| 9.2.4 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |
| 8.14.8 | OSS |
| 7.6.9 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |

### Workarounds

Upgrading Gradle is our recommended fix.

If you cannot upgrade immediately:

* **Make the Gradle user home accessible to its owner only.** Run `chmod 700 ~/.gradle`, or the same on the directory set by `GRADLE_USER_HOME`. Other users can then no longer reach the files Gradle creates inside it.
* **Do not run builds on shared, multi-user machines.** Ensure only trusted users have local (same-host) access to a machine where Gradle builds run. On CI, prefer single-tenant, ephemeral runners rather than shared hosts.

After upgrading or applying a workaround, stop the daemons with `gradle --stop` and delete the `registry.bin` files in `<Gradle user home>/daemon/`. A handle opened before the change keeps reading the file until it is replaced.

### Forensics

A process of another user holding a registry file open indicates an attempt. On Linux and macOS, `lsof` lists the processes that have the files open:

    lsof <Gradle user home>/daemon/*/registry.bin

Nothing in Gradle's output tells a build submitted with a stolen token apart from a legitimate one. The daemon log, `<Gradle user home>/daemon/<Gradle version>/daemon-<pid>.out.log`, records every build request the daemon receives, with the directory it was started from:

`Received command: Build{id=<id>, currentDir=<directory>}.`

An entry whose directory or time matches no build you ran indicates that someone else used the daemon. Gradle deletes daemon log files after 14 days by default. Documentation about daemon logs can be found [here](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/gradle_daemon.html#sec:daemon_logs).

> [!IMPORTANT]
> The lack of a log entry cannot be used to conclude no such attack was performed. The presence of a log entry is not a confirmation that an attack happened, but an indication that more investigations are needed.

### References

* [Securing the Build Tool: Protect the Gradle User Home](https://docs.gradle.org/nightly/userguide/securing_build_tool.html#sec:user_home)
* [Information disclosure through temporary directory permissions](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/security/advisories/GHSA-fp8h-qmr5-j4c8)
* [Gradle client trusts the content of the daemon registry](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/security/advisories/GHSA-gqrr-4j89-5267)

1.description:
### Impact

A **Gradle client** (the `gradle`/`gradlew` CLI or an IDE using the Tooling API) finds running **Gradle daemons** through a registry file, which records the address of each daemon and the secret token used to connect to it. By default the registry is in the Gradle user home, and the `org.gradle.daemon.registry.base` property changes its location. This advisory is about a vulnerability in how the client reads and uses this registry.

The `org.gradle.daemon.registry.base` property is honoured when it is set in a project's `gradle.properties`, so a project can make the client read a registry file that the project itself ships. The client trusts the content of that file:

* it deserializes parts of the file with Java serialization;
* it connects to any address listed in the file, including a remote host, although daemons only ever listen locally;
* it sends its request to that address, including the client's environment variables and system properties for a build, and deserializes the replies, also with Java serialization.

When the client is an IDE or another tool using the Tooling API, a crafted reply makes the client load and run code from a jar URL chosen by the attacker, with the privileges of the user.

A project that sets `org.gradle.daemon.registry.base` is not a safe setup: the property makes the client use daemons, and send them its environment, through a file the project chooses, before any build logic runs. Like a project-set `systemProp.gradle.user.home`, it has to be checked before running Gradle on an untrusted project. Gradle did not document it as such, so users who relied on a validated Wrapper for commands that run no build logic, such as `gradle --status` and `gradle --stop`, or on a review of the build scripts before an IDE synchronizes the project, could run code that appears in none of the project's reviewable sources.

Users who open or inspect untrusted repositories, for example pull requests from forks, are the most at risk.

The attacker must get the user to clone the malicious repository, then run Gradle on it or open it in an IDE.

### Patches

The fixed versions harden how the client reads and uses the daemon registry. They do not make a registry location set by a project safe.

The client no longer uses Java serialization to read the daemon registry. It accepts only the address types Gradle itself writes, and fails on anything else. It also connects only to addresses of the local machine and skips any other address listed in the registry. Together with the mutual authentication of the connection that fixes [GHSA-pcp8-98xm-c6pr](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/security/advisories/GHSA-pcp8-98xm-c6pr), this means a local process that is not a Gradle daemon no longer receives the client's request.

`org.gradle.daemon.registry.base` is still honoured in a project's `gradle.properties`, and a local process holding a token from a registry the project ships still receives the client's request. Check for this property before running Gradle on an untrusted project, also with a fixed version, as described under Workarounds.

| Fix version | Availability |
| ---------- | ----------- |
| 9.9.1 | OSS |
| 9.8.3 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |
| 9.7.3 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |
| 9.6.3 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |
| 9.5.3 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |
| 9.4.3 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |
| 9.3.3 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |
| 9.2.3 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |
| 8.14.7 | OSS |
| 7.6.8 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |

### Workarounds

Upgrading Gradle reduces the impact, but does not make a project that sets `org.gradle.daemon.registry.base` safe. With any Gradle version, before running any Gradle command on an untrusted repository or opening it in an IDE:

* **Check the project's `gradle.properties` for `org.gradle.daemon.registry.base`.** A project has no reason to set it; do not run Gradle on a project that does.
* **Check that no daemon registry is committed.** `git ls-files | grep 'registry.bin$'` lists committed registry files.

### Forensics

A repository that exploits this vulnerability sets `org.gradle.daemon.registry.base` in `gradle.properties` and contains a `registry.bin` file. To check a repository's history, including removed files:

    git log --all -p -- '*gradle.properties' | grep 'org.gradle.daemon.registry.base'
    git log --all --name-only --format= | grep 'registry.bin$'

A fixed version reports a crafted registry instead of using it:

* An entry with an address type Gradle does not write fails the command with `Could not read cache value from '<path>/registry.bin'.`, caused by `Unexpected address type <n> in the daemon registry.`
* An entry with an address of another machine is skipped. With `--info`, the client logs `Removing daemon from the registry due to communication failure. Daemon information: …`. With `--debug`, it also logs `Address <address> is not an address of this machine, skipping.`

> [!IMPORTANT]
> The lack of such files in a repository cannot be used to conclude no such attack was performed. Their presence is not a confirmation that an attack happened, but an indication that more investigations are needed.

1.description:
### Impact

A **Gradle client** (the `gradle`/`gradlew` CLI or an IDE using the Tooling API) looks up running **Gradle daemons** in a registry file under the Gradle user home, then connects to an idle daemon over a loopback TCP connection and sends it the build to run. The client authenticates itself to the daemon with a secret token, but the daemon is not authenticated to the client, and the client does not check that the daemon process recorded in the registry is still running. This advisory is about a vulnerability on this communication channel.

When a daemon terminates without removing itself from the registry, for example when it is killed with `kill -9`, stopped by the out-of-memory killer or crashes, its loopback port becomes free while the registry still points to it. Another local user who binds that port receives the next build request from the victim's client. That request contains the client's environment variables, system properties and standard input, which commonly hold credentials and CI tokens. The attacker can then answer with crafted messages that the client deserializes:

* in an IDE or any other Tooling API client, a crafted reply makes the client process load and run code from a jar chosen by the attacker;
* on the command line, deserializing a hostile object graph can lead to code execution in the client, depending on the classes available, or to a denial of service.

Code execution in the client runs with the privileges of the user running the build. This has been demonstrated with a proof-of-concept. This advisory does not publish the proof-of-concept.

Builds running on **shared / multi-user build hosts** are the most at risk. The vulnerability requires a daemon to have terminated abnormally, leaving a stale entry in the registry, and the attacker to listen on that daemon's port when the victim next starts a build or synchronizes a project in an IDE.

This vulnerability is not exploitable from a remote network connection.

### Patches

The client and the daemon now authenticate each other as soon as a connection opens, before any message is exchanged. The connection token in the registry holds two secrets. The client proves it holds the first one, and only then does the daemon answer with the second. The client checks that answer before it sends anything else. A process listening on the port of a terminated daemon cannot produce the daemon's secret. The client therefore drops the connection, removes the stale entry from the registry, and uses or starts another daemon. That process only receives the client's half of the token of a daemon that no longer exists.

The fix depends on the Gradle version used by the build, not on the Tooling API version of the IDE.

| Fix version | Availability |
| ---------- | ----------- |
| 9.9.1 | OSS |
| 9.8.3 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |
| 9.7.3 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |
| 9.6.3 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |
| 9.5.3 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |
| 9.4.3 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |
| 9.3.3 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |
| 9.2.3 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |
| 8.14.7 | OSS |
| 7.6.8 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |

### Workarounds

Upgrading Gradle is our recommended fix.

If you cannot upgrade immediately:

* **Do not run builds on shared, multi-user machines.** Ensure only trusted users have local (same-host) access to a machine where Gradle builds run. On CI, prefer single-tenant, ephemeral runners rather than shared hosts. The attacker must be a co-located local principal to gain access to the Gradle build.
* **Clear the daemon registry after a daemon terminated abnormally, before the next build.** Delete `<Gradle user home>/daemon/<Gradle version>/registry.bin`. This is safe while daemons are running. Clients no longer find the running daemons and start new ones, and the unregistered daemons stop after their idle timeout (3 hours by default). On an affected version, do not use `gradle --status` or `gradle --stop` for this: both connect to every daemon in the registry, including stale entries.

If you cannot apply these mitigations, restrict which users and processes share a host with your builds until you can upgrade.

### Forensics

Gradle's output does not tell a process squatting a daemon's port apart from a daemon whose port is free. Look for the conditions of the attack on the build host instead:

* A daemon that terminated abnormally leaves a log file, `<Gradle user home>/daemon/<Gradle version>/daemon-<pid>.out.log`, that does not end with `Daemon vm is shutting down...` even though process `<pid>` is no longer running. Its port is on the line `Daemon starting at: …, with address: [… port:<port>, …]`.
* A process of another user listening on that port indicates an attempt. On Linux and macOS: `lsof -nP -iTCP:<port> -sTCP:LISTEN`.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> These checks reveal the conditions for the attack, not the attack itself: by default, Gradle does not record which process a client sent its request to. Daemons also terminate abnormally for ordinary reasons, such as the out-of-memory killer, a crash or a machine reboot, so a log file without a shutdown line is not evidence of an attack. A squatting process only shows while it is still listening, and Gradle deletes daemon log files after 14 days by default, so finding neither does not rule out an attack.

* [Deserialization of untrusted Java objects before authentication in the client - daemon communication](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/security/advisories/GHSA-xwqc-3h47-hg64)
* [Project-controlled daemon registry location](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/security/advisories/GHSA-gqrr-4j89-5267)

1.description:
### Impact

When resolving dependencies, Gradle searches repositories in declaration order. If it encounters connection errors, Gradle will disable the repository and fail dependency resolution. This is necessary for both reproducibility and security reasons to prevent dependencies from being resolved from other repositories without warning. 

In previous versions of Gradle, some exceptions were not treated as fatal errors and would not cause a repository to be disabled. Exceptions like `SSLException` or `SSLHandshakeException` are neither handled as fatal exceptions nor as transient failures. Gradle should fail hard on any failure that is not transient, disable the repository and not move on to the next one. 

This behavior could allow an attacker to disrupt the service of a repository and leverage another repository to serve malicious artifacts. This attack requires the attacker to have control over a repository after the disrupted repository.

### Patches

1.description:
### Impact

A **Gradle client** (the `gradle`/`gradlew` CLI or an IDE using the Tooling API) connects to a long-lived **Gradle daemon** over a loopback TCP connection to send build commands. The daemon listens on this port for its entire lifetime. Most commands on that channel are typed and use a custom serializer but messages can request to use Java serialization. The daemon authenticates client commands with a secret token, but it deserializes the incoming message before it verifies that token. This advisory is about a vulnerability on this communication channel.

An attacker who can place bytes on this channel can cause the daemon to deserialize a hostile object graph which can lead to remote code execution in the daemon JVM or a denial of service (a crash or resource exhaustion from a malformed or deeply nested graph). This has been demonstrated with a proof-of-concept. Code execution in the daemon runs with the privileges of the user running the build and exposes in-memory and on-disk secrets available to it. This advisory does not publish the proof-of-concept.

Builds running on **shared / multi-user build hosts** are the most at risk. The vulnerability requires a Gradle daemon to be running and it does not need to be actively building. 

This vulnerability is not exploitable from a remote network connection.

Gradle has updated the daemon protocol to verify the secret token before deserializing untrusted input.

| ---------- | ----------- |
| 9.8.1 | OSS |
| 9.7.2 | [Gradle Security Subscription](https://gradle.org/security-subscription/) |

If a Gradle build used an unresolvable host name, Gradle would continue to work as long as all dependencies could be resolved from another repository. An unresolvable host name could be caused by allowing a repository's domain name registration to lapse or typo-ing the real domain name. 

This behavior could allow an attacker to register a service under the host name used by the build and serve malicious artifacts. The attack requires the repository to be listed before others in the build configuration. 

### Patches

Gradle has introduced a change in behavior in Gradle 9.3.0 and 8.14.4 to stop searching other repositories when encountering these errors. 

Upgrading to either version will protect you against the vulnerabilities described here.

### Workarounds

If you are using strict [repository content filtering](https://docs.gradle.org/9.3.0/userguide/filtering_repository_content.html#header) and / or [dependency verification](https://docs.gradle.org/9.3.0/userguide/dependency_verification.html), your build is safe from the potential vulnerabilities described above.

If you cannot update to a newer Gradle version, configuring [dependency verification](https://docs.gradle.org/9.3.0/userguide/dependency_verification.html) is the best way to make sure your build resolves the dependencies you expect and nothing else.

You should also review which repositories your builds use to check for unused or outdated repository declarations. 

### References
* [Security feature of failing fast on bad repos does not seem to be implemented](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/issues/35927)
* [Repository disabling](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/graph_resolution.html#sec:repository-disabling)
* [Advisory about repositories failing to answer](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/security/advisories/GHSA-mqwm-5m85-gmcv)

More about this type of vulnerabilities:

* https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/494.html

cwes.name: Creation of Temporary File With Insecure Permissions
Creation of Temporary File in Directory with Insecure Permissions

1.description:
### Impact

On Unix-like systems, the system temporary directory can be created with open permissions that allow multiple users to create and delete files within it. Gradle builds could be vulnerable to a local privilege escalation from an attacker quickly deleting and recreating files in the system temporary directory.

Gradle 8.12, only that exact version, had codepaths where the initialization of the underlying native integration library took a default path, relying on copying the binaries to the system temporary directory. Any execution of Gradle exposed this exploit.

If you are on Windows or modern versions of macOS, you are not vulnerable.
If you are on a Unix-like operating system with the ["sticky" bit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sticky_bit) set or [`noexec`](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fstab#Options_common_to_all_filesystems) on your system temporary directory, you are not vulnerable.

### Patches

This problem was [fixed in Gradle 8.12.1](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/pull/32025). Gradle 8.13 release also upgrades to a version of the native library that no longer has that bug.

### Workarounds

On Unix-like operating systems, ensure that the "sticky" bit is set. This only allows the original user (or root) to delete a file. Mounting `/tmp` as `noexec` will prevent Gradle 8.12 from starting.

If you are unable to change the permissions of the system temporary directory, you can move the Java temporary directory by setting the System Property java.io.tmpdir. The new path needs to limit permissions to the build user only.

### References

* [Root cause vulnerability in `native-platform`](https://github.com/gradle/native-platform/security/advisories/GHSA-2xxp-vw2f-p3x8)
* Prior [Gradle vulnerability](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/security/advisories/GHSA-89qm-pxvm-p336)

More about this type of vulnerabilities:

* [CWE-378: Creation of Temporary File With Insecure Permissions](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/378.html)
* [CWE-379: Creation of Temporary File in Directory with Insecure Permissions](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/379.html)

cwes.name: Incorrect Permission Assignment for Critical Resource

1.description:
### Impact
When copying files or creating archives, Gradle does not preserve symbolic links. Instead, Gradle resolves symbolic links to their underlying target file. The permissions of the new file are the permissions of the symbolic link instead of the permissions of the target file.

This can lead to files that have unintended permissions because symbolic links are usually world readable and writeable.

While it is unlikely this impacts the build directly, it may open attack vectors where build artifacts are used or extracted.

### Patches
In Gradle 7.6.3 and 8.4, the permissions of the target file will be used when copying or archiving a symbolic link.

It is recommended that users upgrade to a patched version.

### Workarounds
If you are unable to upgrade to a patched Gradle version, you should [explicitly set permissions for any symbolic links](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/working_with_files.html#sec:setting_file_permissions) when copying or creating an archive.

### References
* [CWE-732](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/732.html)
* [CVE-2023-34042: Incorrect Permission Assignment for spring-security.xsd](https://spring.io/security/cve-2023-34042)
1.summary: Incorrect permission assignment for symlinked files used in copy or archiving operations

cwes.name: Improper Restriction of XML External Entity Reference

1.description:
### Impact

This is a XML external entities (XXE) vulnerability. See [CWE-611](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/611.html) and  [OWASP XXE](https://owasp.org/www-community/vulnerabilities/XML_External_Entity_(XXE)_Processing).

In some cases, when Gradle parses XML files, resolving XML external entities is not disabled. Combined with an Out Of Band XXE attack (OOB-XXE), just parsing XML can lead to exfiltration of local text files to a remote server.

Gradle parses XML files for several purposes. Most of the time, Gradle parses XML files it generated or were already present locally. Only Ivy XML descriptors and Maven POM files can be fetched from remote repositories and parsed by Gradle.

Impacted use-cases in the Gradle Build Tool:

| Use case | Vulnerable | Exploitable remotely |
| :--- | :---: | :---: |
| Ivy descriptor parsing | YES | YES |
| Maven POM parsing | NO | NO |
| Maven Toolchains discovery | YES | NO |
| Generation of Ivy and Maven metadata for publishing | YES | NO |
| Dependency Verification metadata | NO | NO |
| EAR deployment descriptor parsing | YES | NO |
| IntelliJ, Eclipse, VisualStudio, xcode file generation | YES | NO |

In the use-cases above, only Ivy descriptor parsing is exploitable remotely. This would require an attacker to have control over an Ivy repository used by your build or be able to publish a malicious Ivy descriptor to a repository your build uses for a dependency you use.

Other use-cases are either not exploitable because existing measures protect from the XXE vulnerability or are only exploitable from local files. An attacker would need to modify your build or local build tool configuration files to exploit the XXE vulnerability.

Note that the IDE files generation related use cases only refer to using the relative Gradle plugins to generate their configuration. Project import in IntelliJ, Android Studio or Eclipse are not impacted.

### Patches

In Gradle 7.6.3 and 8.4, resolving XML external entities has been disabled for all use cases to protect against this vulnerability. Gradle will now refuse to parse XML files that have XML external entities.

It is recommended that users upgrade to a patched version.

### Workarounds

If you are unable to upgrade to Gradle 7.6.3 or 8.4, you can disable resolving XML external entities by setting [JAXP](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/13/security/java-api-xml-processing-jaxp-security-guide.html#GUID-D97A1F1D-8DDF-4D19-A7E5-99099F27346E) system properties.

This can be done on the command line by adding the following:
```
-Djavax.xml.accessExternalDTD=false -Djavax.xml.accessExternalSchema=false -Djavax.xml.accessExternalStylesheet=false 
```

This can be made persistent by adding the following lines in a `gradle.properties` file:
```
systemProps.javax.xml.accessExternalDTD=false
systemProps.javax.xml.accessExternalSchema=false
systemProps.javax.xml.accessExternalStylesheet=false 
```

### References

* [CWE-611](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/611.html)
* [OWASP XXE](https://owasp.org/www-community/vulnerabilities/XML_External_Entity_(XXE)_Processing)
* [JAXP Security Guide](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/13/security/java-api-xml-processing-jaxp-security-guide.html#GUID-D97A1F1D-8DDF-4D19-A7E5-99099F27346E)

cwes.name: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory
Inclusion of Functionality from Untrusted Control Sphere

1.description:
### Impact

This is a path traversal vulnerability on the Gradle dependency cache.

When Gradle writes a dependency into its dependency cache, it uses the dependency's coordinates to compute a file location. With specially crafted dependency coordinates, Gradle can be made to write files into an unintended location. The file may be written outside the dependency cache or over another file in the dependency cache. 

This vulnerability could be used to poison the dependency cache or overwrite important files elsewhere on the filesystem where the Gradle process has write permissions.

Exploiting this vulnerability requires an attacker to have control over a dependency repository used by the Gradle build or have the ability to modify the build's configuration. It is unlikely that this would go unnoticed. 

### Patches

A fix has been released in Gradle 7.6.2 and 8.2 to protect against this vulnerability. Gradle will refuse to cache dependencies that have path traversal elements in their dependency coordinates.

It is recommended that users upgrade to a patched version.

### Workarounds

If you are unable to upgrade to Gradle 7.6.2 or 8.2, [dependency verification](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/dependency_verification.html) will make this vulnerability more difficult to exploit.

* When metadata verification is enabled, attackers will be required to either sign compromised dependencies with an already trusted key or to modify the dependency verification metadata.
* Tampered files in the dependency cache will be detected after being overwritten
* Builds that use unexpected artifacts will fail, whether the artifact is downloaded or loaded from cache



### References
 
* [CWE-22: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal')](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/22.html)
* [CWE-829: Inclusion of Functionality from Untrusted Control Sphere](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/829.html)
* [CVE-2022-37866](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2022-37866) Ivy cache path traversal
1.summary: Dependency cache path traversal

cwes.name: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory

1.description:
### Impact

This is a path traversal vulnerability when Gradle deals with Tar archives, often referenced as TarSlip, a variant of ZipSlip.

* When unpacking Tar archives, Gradle did not check that files could be written outside of the unpack location. This could lead to important files being overwritten anywhere the Gradle process has write permissions.
* For a build reading Tar entries from a Tar archive, this issue could allow Gradle to disclose information from sensitive files through an arbitrary file read.

To exploit this behavior, an attacker needs to either control the source of an archive already used by the build or modify the build to interact with a malicious archive. It is unlikely that this would go unnoticed.

Gradle uses Tar archives for its [Build Cache](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/build_cache.html). These archives are safe when created by Gradle. But if an attacker had control of a remote build cache server, they could inject malicious build cache entries that leverage this vulnerability. This attack vector could also be exploited if a man-in-the-middle can be performed between the remote cache and the build.

### Patches

A fix has been released in Gradle 7.6.2 and 8.2 to protect against this vulnerability. Starting from these versions, Gradle will refuse to handle Tar archives which contain path traversal elements in a Tar entry name.

It is recommended that users upgrade to a patched version.

### Workarounds

There is no workaround.

* If your build deals with Tar archives that you do not fully trust, you need to inspect them to confirm they do not attempt to leverage this vulnerability.
* If you use the Gradle remote build cache, make sure only trusted parties have write access to it and that connections to the remote cache are properly secured.

### References

* [CWE-22: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal')](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/22.html)
* [Gradle Build Cache](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/build_cache.html)
* [ZipSlip](https://security.snyk.io/research/zip-slip-vulnerability)
1.summary: Path traversal vulnerabilities in handling of Tar archives

cwes.name: Inclusion of Functionality from Untrusted Control Sphere

1.description:
### Impact

This is a collision attack on long IDs (64bits) for PGP keys.

Users of dependency verification in Gradle are vulnerable if they use long IDs for PGP keys in a `trusted-key` or `pgp` element in their [dependency verification metadata file](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/dependency_verification.html#sec:signature-verification).

### Patches

The fix is to fail dependency verification if anything but a fingerprint is used in a trust element in dependency verification metadata.

The problem is fixed in Gradle 8.0 and above. The problem is also patched in Gradle 6.9.4 and 7.6.1.

### Workarounds

Using only full fingerprint IDs for `trusted-key` or `pgp` element in the metadata is a protection against this issue.

### References
- [CWE-829: Inclusion of Functionality from Untrusted Control Sphere](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/829.html)
- [A Confusing Dependency](https://blog.autsoft.hu/a-confusing-dependency/)
- [Dependency Confusion](https://medium.com/@alex.birsan/dependency-confusion-4a5d60fec610)

cwes.name: Inclusion of Functionality from Untrusted Control Sphere

1.description:
### Impact

Dependency verification is a security feature in Gradle Build Tool that was introduced to allow validation of external dependencies either through their checksum or cryptographic signatures.

In some cases, Gradle may skip that verification and accept a dependency that would otherwise fail the build as an untrusted external artifact.

This can occur in two ways:
* When signature verification is disabled but your verification metadata contains entries for dependencies that only have a `gpg` element but no `checksum` element.
* When signature verification is enabled, your verification metadata contains entries for dependencies with a `gpg` element but there is no signature file on the remote repository.

In both cases, the verification will accept the dependency, skipping signature verification and not complaining that the dependency has no checksum entry.

For builds that are vulnerable, there are two risks:
* Dependency poisoning/Dependency confusion: Gradle could download a malicious binary from a repository outside your organization due to name squatting.
* Man In The Middle: If you are still using HTTP only and not HTTPS for downloading dependencies, your build could download a malicious library instead of the expected one.

### Patches

Gradle 7.5 patches this issue by making sure to run checksum verification if signature verification cannot be completed, whatever the reason.

### Workarounds

* Remove all `gpg` elements from dependency verification metadata if you disable signature validation.
* Do not add `gpg` entries for dependencies that do not have signature files.

### References
- [CWE-829: Inclusion of Functionality from Untrusted Control Sphere](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/829.html)
- [A Confusing Dependency](https://blog.autsoft.hu/a-confusing-dependency/)
- [Dependency Confusion](https://medium.com/@alex.birsan/dependency-confusion-4a5d60fec610)

### Questions?
* For security related issues, please email us at security@gradle.com.
* For non-security related issues, please open an issue on [GitHub](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/issues/new/choose).
1.summary: Dependency verification can ignore checksum verification when signature verification cannot be performed

1.description:
### Impact

Dependency verification is a security feature in Gradle Build Tool that was introduced to allow validation of external dependencies either through their checksum or cryptographic signatures.

In some cases, Gradle may skip that verification and accept a dependency that would otherwise fail the build as an untrusted external artifact.

This occurs when dependency verification is disabled on one or more configurations _and_ those configurations have common dependencies with other configurations that have dependency verification enabled. If the configuration that has dependency verification disabled is resolved _first_, Gradle does not verify the common dependencies for the configuration that has dependency verification enabled.

For builds that are vulnerable, there are two risks:
* Dependency poisoning/Dependency confusion: Gradle could download a malicious binary from a repository outside your organization due to name squatting.
* Man In The Middle: If you are still using HTTP only and not HTTPS for downloading dependencies, your build could download a malicious library instead of the expected one.

### Patches
Gradle 7.4 fixes that issue by validating artifacts at least once if they are present in a resolved configuration that has dependency verification active.

### Workarounds
* Do not use `ResolutionStrategy.disableDependencyVerification()` and do not use plugins that use that method to disable dependency verification for a single configuration.
* Make sure resolution of configuration that disable that feature do not happen in builds that resolve configuration where the feature is enabled.

- [CWE-829: Inclusion of Functionality from Untrusted Control Sphere](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/829.html)

cwes.name: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command

1.description:
### Impact

[Start scripts generated by the `application` plugin](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/application_plugin.html#header) and the [`gradlew` script](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/gradle_wrapper.html#header) are both vulnerable to arbitrary code execution when an attacker is able to change environment variables for the user running the script.

This may impact you if you use `gradlew` on Unix-like systems or use the scripts generated by Gradle in your application on Unix-like systems.

For `gradlew`, commands can be included in either `JAVA_OPTS` or `GRADLE_OPTS`.
For start scripts, commands can be included in either `JAVA_OPTS` or `<APP_NAME>_OPTS`.

For example, if a command is added to `JAVA_OPTS` and the user runs a Gradle build:
```
$ export JAVA_OPTS='-Xmx512m $(touch foo)' 
$ ./gradlew build
```

This will execute `touch foo`, but any command will work here. When determining the command-line for the Java process that is started by the script, any commands found in these environment variables will be executed as the user running the script.

For this vulnerability to be exploitable, an attacker needs to be able to set the value of particular environment variables and have those environment variables be seen by the vulnerable scripts. 

This vulnerability was found during a security audit. We do not know of any exploits based on this vulnerability.

### Patches

This issue has been patched in Gradle 7.2 by updating our start script template.

### Workarounds

#### CI/CD systems using the Gradle build tool

You are not vulnerable if untrusted users are unable to change environment variables for the user that executes `gradlew`.

If you are unable to upgrade to Gradle 7.2, you can generate a new `gradlew` script with Gradle 7.2 and use it for older versions of Gradle. 

#### Applications using start scripts generated by Gradle

You are not vulnerable if untrusted users are unable to change environment variables for the user that executes the start script.

If you are unsure, the vulnerable start script could be manually patched to remove the use of `eval` or the use of environment variables that affect the application's command-line.

If the application is simple enough, you may be able to avoid the use of the start scripts by running the application directly with Java command.

### References
- [Eval command and security issues](https://mywiki.wooledge.org/BashFAQ/048)
- [The perils of Bash 'eval'](https://medium.com/dot-debug/the-perils-of-bash-eval-cc5f9e309cae)

### Questions?
* For security related issues, please email us at security@gradle.com.
* For non-security related issues, please open an issue on [GitHub](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/issues/new/choose).

1.description:
### Impact

Files created with open permissions in the system temporary directory can allow an attacker to access information downloaded by Gradle. Some builds could be vulnerable to a local information disclosure.

Remote files accessed through [`TextResourceFactory`](https://docs.gradle.org/current/dsl/org.gradle.api.resources.TextResourceFactory.html) are downloaded into the system temporary directory first. Sensitive information contained in these files can be exposed to other local users on the same system.

If you do not use the `TextResourceFactory` API, you are not vulnerable. 

### What should you do? 

### Upgrade to Gradle 7.0

As of Gradle 7.0, uses of the system temporary directory have been moved to the Gradle User Home directory. By default, this directory is restricted to the user running the build. 

#### Workarounds for older versions

Set a more restrictive [umask](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umask) that removes read access to other users. When files are created in the system temporary directory, they will not be accessible to other users. 

If you are unable to change your system's umask, you can move the Java temporary directory by setting the System Property `java.io.tmpdir`. The new path needs to limit permissions to the build user only.

### References
- Vulnerable code: https://github.com/gradle/gradle/blob/ad8c7c993bda8c2660ddd36584b2d2a035cc2e8c/subprojects/core/src/main/java/org/gradle/api/internal/resources/ApiTextResourceAdapter.java#L65-L72 
- [CWE-377: Insecure Temporary File](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/377.html)

1.description:
### Impact

On Unix-like systems, the system temporary directory can be created with open permissions that allow multiple users to create and delete files within it. Gradle builds could be vulnerable to a local privilege escalation from an attacker quickly deleting and recreating files in the system temporary directory. 

This vulnerability impacted builds using [precompiled script plugins written in Kotlin DSL](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/custom_plugins.html#sec:precompiled_plugins) and tests for Gradle plugins written using [`ProjectBuilder`](https://docs.gradle.org/current/javadoc/org/gradle/testfixtures/ProjectBuilder.html) or [TestKit](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/test_kit.html).

If you are on Windows or modern versions of macOS, you are not vulnerable.
If you are on a Unix-like operating system with the ["sticky" bit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sticky_bit) set on your system temporary directory, you are not vulnerable.

#### Precompiled script plugins 

When compiling precompiled script plugins written in Kotlin DSL, Gradle uses a temporary directory in the system temporary directory to execute a build-like process. 

A local privilege escalation can occur due to a race condition in the creation of this temporary directory. If an attacker is able to write files into the directory created by Gradle, the attacker can execute commands at the same privilege level as the build. 

If you do not use precompiled script plugins, you are not vulnerable.

#### `ProjectBuilder` API in tests

`ProjectBuilder` is most commonly used by plugin authors to write unit tests. With this API, if you do not [specify a project directory](https://docs.gradle.org/current/javadoc/org/gradle/testfixtures/ProjectBuilder.html#withProjectDir-java.io.File-), Gradle will create one for you in a temporary directory.

A local privilege escalation can occur due to a race condition in the creation of this temporary directory. If an attacker is able to write files into the project directory created for the test, the attacker can execute commands at the same privilege level as the build. 

If you do not use `ProjectBuilder` or you always specify a project directory, you are not vulnerable.

#### Gradle TestKit in tests

TestKit is also used by plugin authors to write integration tests. These tests execute full Gradle builds. TestKit uses a well-known path in the system temporary directory to cache some information between runs, like Gradle distributions and dependency downloads.

A local privilege escalation can occur if an attacker controls the creation of this directory. If an attacker is able to write files into the directory created for TestKit, the attacker can execute commands at the same privilege level as the build. 

If you do not use TestKit, you are not vulnerable.

### What should you do? 

### Upgrade to Gradle 7.0

As of Gradle 7.0, `ProjectBuilder`, TestKit and other uses of the system temporary directory have been removed where possible. Instead of relying on the system temporary directory, Gradle now uses a combination of the Gradle User Home and project's build directory.

#### Workaround for older versions

On Unix-like operating systems, ensure that the "sticky" bit is set. This only allows the original user (or root) to delete a file.

If you are unable to change the permissions of the system temporary directory, you can move the Java temporary directory by setting the System Property `java.io.tmpdir`. The new path needs to limit permissions to the build user only.

 - JUnit 4 - https://github.com/junit-team/junit4/security/advisories/GHSA-269g-pwp5-87pp

1.description:
We want to thank [Marcin Zajączkowski](https://github.com/szpak) who originally reported this vulnerability to us.

### Impact
Users that sign artifacts using the built-in [signing plugin with gpg-agent](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/signing_plugin.html#sec:using_gpg_agent) may be affected. If you do not sign your artifacts, you are not affected.

At `INFO` and `DEBUG` level logging, Gradle prints the full command-line of every executed process. When signing artifacts with gpg, Gradle executes the `gpg` or `gpg2` command-line tool and passes the passphrase for the private key as an argument. When `INFO` and `DEBUG` level logging is enabled, Gradle inadvertently logs the passphrase to the build log.

Users signing artifacts with gpg-agent are vulnerable with Gradle 4.5 through Gradle 6.4.x.

### Patches

This behavior has been patched in Gradle 6.5.

### Workarounds
If you are unable to upgrade, there are a few possible workarounds or mitigations:

1. Check that your CI system is masking your passphrase from logs
1. Check that your CI system is not using INFO or DEBUG level logging

We want to thank [Vladimir Sitnikov](https://github.com/vlsi) who originally reported this vulnerability to us and contributed a fix.

### Impact

Users publishing to artifact servers like Maven Central are required to upload files signed with GPG/PGP and a `.asc` file containing the signature.

Before Gradle 6.0, the `signing` plugin that created these `.asc` files used a SHA1 digest, which is considered cryptographically broken and is known to be vulnerable to second-preimage attacks. Note that `.asc` file embeds its own digest and it is not related to checksum `.sha1` and `.md5` files.

Users who are concerned that their upstream artifact servers may be compromised use GPG/PGP signatures to verify that artifacts are legitimate. You can read more about this type of vulnerability at [CWE-327: Use of a Broken or Risky Cryptographic Algorithm](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/327.html).

### Patches

This vulnerability has been fixed in [Gradle 6.0](https://gradle.org/releases/).

### Workarounds
If you are unable to upgrade the version of Gradle you are using, you can consider doing the following: 

 - Use [gpg executable](https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/signing_plugin.html#sec:using_gpg_agent) for signing, and ensure it defaults to strong digests. Gradle 5.x requires that you specify a signing key id via signing.gnupg.keyName property when using gpg executable (see https://github.com/gradle/gradle/issues/8657).
 - Ask your users to check multiple checksums like SHA1 and MD5 (both are required by Maven Central). Although both of these hashing algorithms are considered cryptographically broken, creating a malicious file that matches both a published SHA1 and MD5 hash has not yet been publicly proven to have occurred yet.
 - Publish stronger checksums like SHA256 or SHA512.

### How do I check if an `.asc` file is using SHA1?

You can use gpg or pgpdump utilities to verify if a given `.asc` file is strong or not.

Using `gpg`, the following command prints "digest algo 2" when a SHA1 digest is used.
```
gpg --list-packets file.jar.asc
```

Using `pgpdump`, the following command prints "Hash alg - SHA1(hash 2)" when a SHA1 digest is used.
```
pgpdump file.jar.asc
```

### For more information

* [Maven Centrals PGP signature requirements](https://central.sonatype.org/pages/working-with-pgp-signatures.html).
* Apache Software Foundation recommends users [avoid SHA1 digest for PGP signatures](https://www.apache.org/dev/openpgp.html#sha1). 
* For security related issues, please email us at security@gradle.com.
* For non-security related issues, please open an issue on [GitHub](https://github.com/gradle/gradle/issues/new/choose).
